core: Working definition of coping as the mental and behavioral efforts used to manage stress and its demands
Problem-focused versus emotion-focused coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984): change the problem vs change the feeling
Five named strategies — planning, seeking support, reframing, distraction, avoidance — each with an original example, plus the honest note that avoidance helps short-term only
Fit between coping strategy and situation (controllability) as what makes coping work
Social support as a coping resource: practical help, advice, emotional comfort
Honest note: there is no one right way to cope
Honest framing: coping is stress management, not stress elimination
supporting: Perceived control and its role in choosing a coping approach
Reappraisal as the mechanism behind reframing
Social support as a general protective factor for health
outOfScope: The stress response itself and the types of stressors (sibling topic: stress)
Stress-management practice and clinical interventions (nursing subject)
Treatment of stress-related conditions, psychotherapy techniques, and medication (psychology subject: mental-health-treatment-overview)

claims.claim: Coping is the use of mental and behavioral efforts to manage the demands of stress — cognitive and behavioral strategies for dealing with a situation appraised as taxing or exceeding one's resources, and for reducing the negative emotions and conflict stress causes.

Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman (1984) distinguished two fundamental kinds of coping: problem-focused coping, which attempts to manage or alter the stressor itself, and emotion-focused coping, which attempts to change or reduce the negative emotions associated with stress.

Problem-focused coping is used primarily when a person appraises a stressor as within their capacity to change, while emotion-focused coping predominates when the stressor is appraised as beyond their control; emotion-focused coping is more effective for uncontrollable stressors.

Emotion-focused coping includes reframing (reappraisal — construing the stressor differently without changing its objective level of threat) and distraction-type moves that take the mind off the situation.

Avoidance coping disengages from the stressor and averts attention from it; it may provide some benefit by reducing stress and preventing anxiety from becoming overwhelming in the short term, but it does not address the problem itself and is generally viewed more unfavorably than approach coping.

Social support — practical help, advice and guidance, and emotional comfort that makes a person feel valued, accepted, and understood — helps people cope with stress, and social relationships are a protective factor for health.
There is no single best coping strategy; effective coping depends on the fit between the strategy and the situation, and coping manages stress rather than eliminating it.

positions: Avoidant strategies may provide some benefit by reducing stress and preventing anxiety from becoming overwhelming (APA Dictionary of Psychology, avoidance coping)
Avoidance is generally viewed more unfavorably than approach coping because it leaves the stressor unaddressed, so the problem tends to persist or grow
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the honest two-sided note: avoidance offers short-term relief but does not change the stressor, so it fails as a long-term strategy. No quantitative claim is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are problem-focused and emotion-focused coping alternatives or companions?
positions: The two families are sometimes presented as distinct approaches a person might choose between
Many stressors elicit both kinds of coping, often at the same time (OpenStax Psychology 2e, 14.4)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the distinction as a classification, not a contest, and states plainly that people commonly use both.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft made no verifiable factual claims about coping ('Coping is a foundational concept in Psychology', 'a college-level explanation names the concept', 'label on a toolbox drawer' analogy); all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's boilerplate with a source-verified lesson: the working definition follows OpenStax 14.4 and the APA Dictionary; the problem-focused/emotion-focused distinction is attributed to Lazarus and Folkman (1984); avoidance's short-term-only note follows the APA Dictionary's avoidance coping entry.
Removed the draft's banned boilerplate phrases and the generic 'toolbox drawer' analogy.
All examples, scenarios, and practice questions are original; no statistics were invented or reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, 14.4 Regulation of Stress
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read live at the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supplies the working definition of coping (mental and behavioral efforts to deal with problems relating to stress), the Lazarus & Folkman (1984) problem-/emotion-focused distinction, reappraisal as emotion-focused coping, the controllability/fit point (problem-focused for controllable stressors, emotion-focused more effective for uncontrollable ones), and social support as advice, guidance, encouragement, emotional comfort, and tangible assistance. Reference only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: coping
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A reference. Read via the dictionary's public content API on 2026-08-22. Confirms the working definition: use of cognitive and behavioral strategies to manage demands appraised as taxing or exceeding one's resources, or to reduce the negative emotions and conflict caused by stress.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: problem-focused coping
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A reference. Read via the dictionary's public content API on 2026-08-22. Confirms the definition (directly confronting the stressor, generating solutions, instrumental action), the 1984 Lazarus & Folkman attribution, and the proposal that problem-focused coping is used when the stressor is appraised as within one's capacity to change.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: emotion-focused coping
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A reference. Read via the dictionary's public content API on 2026-08-22. Confirms the definition (regulating negative emotional reactions rather than changing the stressor), tools including positive reframing and relaxation, the 1984 Lazarus & Folkman attribution, and the proposal that emotion-focused coping is used when the stressor is appraised as beyond one's capacity to change.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: social support
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A reference. Read via the dictionary's public content API on 2026-08-22. Confirms the forms of support: practical help, tangible assistance, and emotional support that makes a person feel valued, accepted, and understood.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: avoidance coping
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A reference. Read via the dictionary's public content API on 2026-08-22. Confirms the definition (disengaging from the stressor and averting attention from it) and the honest two-sided note that avoidant strategies may reduce stress short-term and prevent anxiety from becoming overwhelming, while being generally viewed more unfavorably than approach coping.

sourceRecords.title: The Healthy Life
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook (Noba, live 2026-08-22; module by Emily Hooker and Sarah Pressman). Corroborates the problem-focused/emotion-focused classification of coping and the protective role of social relationships (emotional help, tangible help, advice). Used for corroboration only; reference only.
